title: Intestinal Lactobacillus murinus -derived small RNAs target porcine polyamine metabolism
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

sections.abstract:
Polyamine metabolism participates in various processes of host physiology and disease. The roles of intrinsic factors in polyamine metabolism have been well clarified, but the effects of extrinsic factors, such as gut microbes, on polyamine metabolism remain elusive. Here, we found the intestinal Lactobacillus murinus -derived small RNAs in extracellular vesicles down-regulate host polyamine metabolism by inhibiting the expression of enzymes in polyamine metabolism. The intestinal microbiota-derived small RNAs–host polyamine metabolism axis is associated with the pathogenesis of colitis and colorectal cancer. These findings enhance our understanding of polyamine metabolism and suggest possible avenues for therapeutic interventions in polyamine-related diseases.

Keywords: colitis, CRC, Lactobacillus murinus , polyamine metabolism, small RNAs

sections.results:
Gut microbiota modulates tryptophan metabolism with GF pigs ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 A ) ( 11 ); however, it is unclear whether gut microbiota is involved in host polyamine metabolism ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 B ). Therefore, we performed targeted metabolomics to analyze the level of putrescine, spermidine, and spermine in the intestinal segments and their contents, feces, extraintestinal organs (heart, liver, spleen, and kidney), and circulatory system (serum and urine and bile) of GF pigs with or without fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). There was no change in the level of polyamines in the serum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, jejunal contents, heart, kidney, and bile ( Fig. 1 A and SI Appendix , Fig. S1 C–E ). The putrescine level was decreased in the cecal contents, colonic contents, and feces of GF pigs ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 C ), which is consistent with the previous study demonstrating lower putrescine level in the feces of GF mice ( 14 ). In addition, we also found a diminished level of spermidine in the liver and lower level of putrescine in the spleen of GF pigs ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 D ). In contrast, the level of spermine in the urine ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 E ) and level of spermidine and total polyamines were up-regulated in the colon of GF pigs ( Fig. 1 A ). These results suggest that gut microbiota alters host polyamine metabolism in a tissue-dependent manner. We then validated this observation with GF mice ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 F ). There was higher level of putrescine and spermine in the serum and higher level of spermine in the duodenum of GF mice ( Fig. 1 B and C ). Meanwhile, spermidine and spermine were up-regulated in the colon of GF mice compared with SPF mice ( Fig. 1 D ), accompanied by higher mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM ( Fig. 1 E ). Meanwhile, increased ODC1 and AMD1 protein abundance were observed in the colon of GF mice ( Fig. 1 F ). Collectively, our data suggest that the absence of gut microbiota leads to increased polyamine levels in the colon.

Gut microbiota is involved in host polyamine metabolism. ( A ) The level of putrescine, spermidine, spermine, and polyamines in the serum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, and colon of FMT and GF pigs (n = 7 to 13). ( B – D ) The level of putrescine, spermidine, spermine, and polyamines in the serum ( B ), duodenum ( C ), and colon ( D ) of SPF and GF mice (n = 14 to 20). ( E ) mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM in the colon of SPF and GF mice (n = 4). ( F ) Protein abundance of ODC1 and AMD1 in the colon of SPF and GF mice (n = 4). Data were analyzed by unpaired t test or Mann–Whitney U test [A: Colon (Polyamines), B: Putrescine, Spermidine, Spermine, Polyamines, C: Spermine, D: Putrescine, Spermine] and represented as mean ± SD ( A – D , F ) or SEM ( E ). * P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01; *** P < 0.001; **** P < 0.0001.

To determine whether eliminating part of the gut microbiota would phenocopy the profile of polyamine metabolism in GF models, we treated mice with neomycin, ampicillin, metronidazole, colistin, or vancomycin for two weeks, respectively ( Fig. 2 A ). Fecal samples at day 14 were subjected to 16S rRNA gene sequencing. There was altered intestinal microbiota composition among groups based on the alpha-diversity, beta-diversity, and principal coordinates (PCoA) analysis ( SI Appendix , Fig. S2 A – D ). Comparative analyses were performed to identify the taxa with significantly altered relative abundance at the phylum and genus levels ( SI Appendix , Fig. S2 E and F ). These results revealed that antibiotic administration alters gut microbial composition in mice. Next, targeted metabolomics was performed to analyze the polyamines in the serum and colon. Increased polyamine levels were observed in the serum of mice treated with ampicillin, metronidazole, colistin, or vancomycin ( Fig. 2 B ). Notably, higher level of putrescine, spermidine, and spermine was detected in the colon of mice with colistin administration ( Fig. 2 C ). Meanwhile, higher ODC1, AMD1, and SRM mRNA expression ( Fig. 2 D ) and increased ODC1 and AMD1 protein abundance were observed in the colon of mice with colistin administration ( Fig. 2 E ). Overall, these results indicate that the altered microbiota composition in colistin-treated mice is linked to host polyamine metabolism.

Colistin-induced alteration of gut microbiota is linked to polyamine metabolism. ( A ) A schematic diagram of the antibiotic-treated mouse model. ( B and C ) The level of putrescine, spermidine, spermine, and polyamines in the serum ( B ) and colon ( C ) of control and antibiotic-treated mice (n = 8 to 12). ( D ) Real-time RT-PCR analysis of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM mRNA expression in the colon of control and colistin-treated mice (n = 9 to 12). ( E ) Protein abundance of ODC1 and AMD1 in the colon of control and colistin-treated mice (n = 4 to 5). Data were analyzed by unpaired t test or Mann–Whitney U test (B Putrescine: Colistin; B Spermidine: Vancomycin; B Spermine: Neomycin, ampicillin, metronidazole, colistin or vancomycin; B Polyamines: Vancomycin; C Putrescine: Neomycin, ampicillin, metronidazole, colistin, or vancomycin; C Spermidine: Neomycin, ampicillin, metronidazole, colistin, or vancomycin; C Spermine: Neomycin, ampicillin, metronidazole, colistin, or vancomycin; C Polyamines: Neomycin, ampicillin, metronidazole, colistin, or vancomycin; D: ODC1, E: AMD1) and represented as mean ± SD ( B , C , and E ) or SEM ( D ). * P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01; *** P < 0.001; **** P < 0.0001.

To determine bacterial communities with statistical differences between the colistin and control group, we conducted linear discriminant analysis (LDA) effect size (LEfSe). Colistin administration resulted in a loss of L. murinus , Lactobacillus johnsonii, and Lactobacillus reuteri ( Fig. 3 A ). To further identify the gut microbes underlying the alteration of polyamine levels, we conducted Spearman’s correlation analysis between polyamine levels and microbial species richness. We found a significant negative correlation between L. murinus and polyamine levels in the serum and colon ( Fig. 3 B ), suggesting low abundance of L. murinus is associated with increased polyamine levels.

L. murinus (F5) diminishes level of polyamines in vivo. ( A ) LEfSe analysis shows bacterial taxa that are significantly different in abundance between mice with or without colistin administration (n = 10). ( B ) Spearman’s correlation between the top 10 species and metabolomic data of putrescine, spermidine, and spermine in the serum and colon (n = 10). ( C and D ) The level of putrescine, spermidine, spermine, and polyamines in the serum ( C ) and colon ( D ) of mice colonized with or without F5 (n = 8 to 12). ( E and F ) The level of putrescine, spermidine, spermine, and polyamines in the serum ( E ) and colon ( F ) of GF mice monocolonized with or without F5 (n = 12). Data were analyzed by unpaired t test or Mann–Whitney U test (F: Putrescine) and represented as mean ± SD ( C – F ). * P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01; **** P < 0.0001.

To further understand the roles of L. murinus in polyamine metabolism, we isolated L. murinus (F5) from the feces of ICR mice ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 A ), which shared 100% identity with the V4–V5 16S region of OTU of the representative sequence of L. murinus . Next, we colonized F5 or L. reuteri (as negative control) in mice pretreated with an antibiotic cocktail ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 B ). Metabolomics revealed that mice colonized with F5 showed diminished polyamine levels in the serum and colon ( Fig. 3 C and D ). As a control, L. reuteri administration did not decrease polyamine levels in the serum and colon ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 C and D ). To further validate the role of F5 in polyamine metabolism, GF mice were monocolonized with F5 ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 E ). GF mice monocolonized with F5 showed lower polyamine levels in the colon compared with GF controls, while no change of polyamine levels was observed in the serum ( Fig. 3 E and F ), which may be related to the period of F5 administration. Collectively, F5 down-regulates colonic polyamine levels in vivo.

Then, we explored the potential mechanism of how F5 down-regulates polyamine levels. As L. amylovorus utilizes amino acids, making itself dominant in the small intestine ( 15 ); we therefore hypothesized that the F5 utilizes arginine (the precursor of polyamines) in the intestinal lumen, thus limiting host polyamine biosynthesis. To test this hypothesis, we cultured F5 in MRS broth supplemented with different dosages of arginine. We found that 0.5% or 1% arginine supplementation suppressed the growth of L. murinus at 12 and 24 h ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 A ). Notably, the arginine, ornithine, and polyamine levels in the F5 culture supernatant increased substantially at 24 h ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 B ), suggesting that F5 produces arginine and polyamines. Notably, F5 cultured in MRS broth supplemented with polyamines displayed decreased growth at 6, 12, and 24 h ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 C ), indicating that excessive polyamines in the environment inhibit the growth of F5 at a later stage.

To elucidate the underlying mechanism by which F5 down-regulates host polyamine levels, we cocultured F5-derived metabolites, live F5, or pasteurized F5 with IPEC-J2 cells (intestinal porcine epithelial cells) for 4 h in vitro ( SI Appendix , Fig. S5 A ). Notably, we found that pasteurized F5 down-regulated polyamine levels in the coculture system ( Fig. 4 A ). Pasteurized F5 also inhibited mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM ( Fig. 4 B ), as well as protein abundance of ODC1 and AMD1 in IPEC-J2 cells ( Fig. 4 C ). These data suggested that pasteurized F5 down-regulates polyamine metabolism, which was further supported by disintegrating F5 using sonication before coculture with IPEC-J2 cells ( SI Appendix , Fig. S5 B ).

F5-derived small RNAs target polyamine metabolism. ( A ) The level of putrescine, spermidine, spermine, and polyamines in the supernatant of coculture systems (n = 5 to 6). ( B ) mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM in IPEC-J2 cells cocultured with or without pasteurized F5 (10 8 ) (n = 5 to 12). ( C ) Protein abundance of ODC1 and AMD1 in IPEC-J2 cells cocultured with or without pasteurized F5 (10 8 ) (n = 3 to 4). ( D ) mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM in IPEC-J2 cells cocultured with or without cell-free supernatant, pasteurized F5 (10 8 ), pasteurized F5 (10 8 ) pretreated with DNA remover, or pasteurized F5 (10 8 ) pretreated with RNase A (n = 6 to 12). ( E ) The level of putrescine, spermidine, spermine, and polyamines in supernatant of coculture systems (n = 6). ( F ) mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM in IPEC-J2 cells cocultured with or without pasteurized F5 (10 8 ), pasteurized F5 (10 8 ) pretreated with RNase A or RNAs with more than 200 nt in length isolated from F5 (n = 5 to 6). ( G ) mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM in IPEC-J2 cells cocultured with or without RNAs with 20 to 200 nt in length isolated from F5 (n = 5 to 6). ( H ) Protein abundance of ODC1 and AMD1 in IPEC-J2 cells cocultured with or without RNAs with 20 to 200 nt in length isolated from F5 (n = 3 to 4). Data were analyzed by unpaired t test ( B , C , G , and H ) or one-way ANOVA ( A and D – F ) and represented as mean ± SD ( A , C , E , and H ) or SEM ( B , D , F , and G ).

To identify the components of pasteurized F5 that regulate polyamine metabolism, we pretreated pasteurized F5 with DNase, RNase A, and proteinase K before coculture with IPEC-J2 cells. We found that RNase A pretreatment abolished the down-regulation of mRNA expression and polyamine levels induced by pasteurized F5 ( Fig. 4 D and E and SI Appendix , Fig. S5 C ). These findings revealed that the small RNAs from pasteurized F5 down-regulate polyamine metabolism. Next, we extracted RNAs with more than 200 nt or 20 to 200 nt in length from F5 for the coculture. RNAs with more than 200 nt in length failed to decrease mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM in IPEC-J2 cells ( Fig. 4 F ), whereas RNAs with 20 to 200 nt in length decreased mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM in IPEC-J2 cells ( Fig. 4 G ). Meanwhile, RNAs with 20 to 200 nt in length decreased the protein abundance of ODC1 and AMD1 in IPEC-J2 cells ( Fig. 4 H ). These results suggested that RNAs with 20 to 200 nt in length derived from F5 down-regulate polyamine metabolism.

Next, we wanted to identify exact small RNAs targeting polyamine metabolism, we therefore performed small RNA sequencing. We showed the counts of raw reads, clean reads, and unique clean reads in IPEC-J2 cells cocultured with or without pasteurized F5 ( Fig. 5 A ). Next, we aligned the clean reads with the reference genome of Ligilactobacillus murinus . We obtained the counts of reads ( Fig. 5 B ) and unique reads ( Fig. 5 C ) that derived from L. murinus , which was distributed with 18 to 32 nt in length ( SI Appendix , Fig. S6 A ). We reported 15534 reads that came from L. murinus according to the detection standard of exogenous RNAs (q value < 0.0001 and FC > 100) ( SI Appendix , Fig. S6 B ). The gene ontology (GO) and kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG) enrichment results of F5-derived reads contained certain enriched pathways related to signal transduction, transporter activity, and binding ( SI Appendix , Fig. S6 C and D ). Next, we predicted the targets of differentially expressed small RNAs using Miranda. We found 14, 1, and 24 reads targeting ODC1 , AMD1 and SRM , respectively ( Fig. 5 D ). Then, we calculated the abundance of those identified small RNAs using script per million (TPM) as a metric ( Fig. 5 E ). Next, agarose gel electrophoresis was performed for the further validation of the existence of sR-182871 (targeting ODC 1), sR-242825 (targeting AMD1 ), and sR-257800 (targeting SRM ) in the pasteurized F5 and IPEC-J2 cells cocultured with pasteurized F5 ( Fig. 5 F ).

( B ) The counts of total reads and reads mapped to the representative genome of L. murinus in IPEC-J2 cells (n = 3). Data were analyzed by unpaired t test and represented as mean ± SEM ( L , M , and O – S ).

Next, we wanted to know by which pathway F5 releases and transports small RNA. Bacterial extracellular vesicles (bEVs) are commonly produced by bacteria for the purpose of long-distance transmission of bacterial molecules, which is one of the methods that affect the interaction between bacteria and host and is considered to be a genuine secretion system ( 16 ). Our transmission electron microscopy results showed that F5 released EVs ( Fig. 5 G ) which contains sR-182871, sR-242825, and sR-257800 ( Fig. 5 H and I ). EVs production by Gram-positive bacteria involves peptidoglycan-degrading enzymes that lead to explosive cell lysis ( 17 , 18 ). To test this, the culture supernatant of F5 was collected at 0 h, 4 h, and 24 h for the detection of sR-182871, sR-242825, and sR-257800, meanwhile the dead proportion of F5 at these time points was also monitored. We found that the level of sR-182871, sR-242825, and sR-257800 became higher gradually along with the increased proportion of dead F5 ( Fig. 5 J ), indicating that the release of small RNA may be associated with bacterial lysis. Next, we demonstrated that these small RNAs released by F5 were indeed small RNAs rather than randomly degraded fragments of mRNA with following evidence: 1) We found that sR-242825, sR-182871, and sR-257800 were detected at almost stable abundance in different samples among various replicates ( Fig. 5 K ); 2) sR-242825, sR-182871, and sR-257800 were detected at similar levels in the colon of mice with different species ( SI Appendix , Fig. S6 E ).

To determine whether the physiological concentration of selected small RNAs is enough to regulate the polyamine metabolism in mammalian cells, we first determined the absolute level of sR-257800 [as the abundance of sR-257800 is the lowest compared with that of sR-242825, sR-182871( Fig. 5 K )] in the colon of mice under normal physiological conditions. The absolute level of sR-257800 in the colon of mice under normal physiological conditions was (0.9–3.4) × 10 −3 pmol/mg colon tissue [equivalent to (1.8–6.8) × 10 −9 pmol/cell] ( SI Appendix , Fig. S6 F ). Thus, mimics of sR-242825, sR-182871, and sR-257800 were synthesized and added to IPEC-J2 cells at physiological concentration of sR-257800. The intracellular small RNAs concentration at 1.08 × 10 −9 pmol/cell and 6.18 × 10 −9 pmol/cell diminished mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM ( Fig. 5 L ), as well as the protein abundance of ODC1 and AMD1 in IPEC-J2 cells ( Fig. 5 M ), indicating that the physiological concentration of selected small RNAs is enough to regulate polyamine metabolism in mammalian cells. To uncover the location of small RNAs in target cells, we labeled the sR-242825 (Cy5) and found that small RNAs were mainly located at cytoplasm aggregating near the nucleus ( Fig. 5 N ). To understand how selected small RNAs interact with target genes, miRanda and RNAhybrid websites were used for target prediction. The putative binding sites of sR-242825 and sR-257800 were located in the 3′ untranslated region (3′UTR) of the AMD1 and SRM transcripts, respectively ( SI Appendix , Fig. S6 G and H ). The binding of sR-242825 with AMD1 and sR-257800 with SRM were further demonstrated with luciferase assay ( Fig. 5 O and P ).

We further analyzed the abundance of sR-182871, sR-242825, and sR-257800 in models with altered polyamine metabolism ( SI Appendix , Figs. S1 F, S2 A , and S3 E ). As expected, GF and colistin-treated mice, which showed higher polyamine levels in the colon ( Figs. 1 D and 2 C ), had a lower abundance of sR-182871, sR-242825, and sR-257800 in the colon ( Fig. 5 Q and R ). Notably, the GF mice monocolonized with F5, which showed declined polyamine levels in the colon ( Fig. 3 H ), showed a higher abundance of sR-182871, sR-242825, and sR-257800 in the colon ( Fig. 5 S ). Further, the abundance of sR-257800 in the coculture system composed of IPEC-J2 cells and pasteurized F5 was about 115 times to that in the coculture system composed of IPEC-J2 cells and live F5 ( Fig. 5 T ). These results indicate that F5-derived small RNAs target the expression of enzymes in polyamine metabolism, resulting in diminished polyamine levels.

Polyamines are implicated in cell growth and tissue regeneration and promote proliferation of colon epithelial cells ( 19 ), thus ameliorating symptoms of DSS-induced colitis in mice ( 14 ). We thus assumed that the F5 delays colitis recovery via decreasing polyamines. We challenged mice with 3.2% DSS for 8 days, followed by oral gavage with anaerobic PBS, F5 suspension, or F5 suspension with polyamines for 6 days ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 A ). DSS reduced mouse body weight on day 8 ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 B ). Importantly, F5 colonization ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 C ) induced a lower body weight over the recovery stage ( Fig. 6 A ) and a decline in colon length ( Fig. 6 B ) and colon weight ( Fig. 6 C ) in mice. Moreover, mice in DSS + F5 group showed higher expression of sR-182871, sR-242825, and sR-257800 ( Fig. 6 D ) but lower expression of enzymes in polyamine metabolism ( Fig. 6 E and F ) and polyamine levels ( Fig. 6 G ) in the colon. Notably, polyamine supplementation rescued these indicators ( Fig. 6 A – G ), suggesting that lower polyamine levels induced by F5 delays the recovery of colitis. The lower abundance of L. murinus in the feces after polyamine supplementation ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 C ) was consistent with the observation in vitro that polyamines inhibited growth of L. murinus at late stage ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 C ).

Polyamines play crucial roles in the pathogenesis of colitis and CRC. To understand the underlying reason that polyamine deficiency delays colitis recovery, we performed hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and did not observe appreciable changes in intestinal epithelium structure among groups ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 D ). M2 macrophages are tightly associated with polyamine metabolism and are also involved in the recovery from colitis ( 20 ). We analyzed the mRNA expression of MRC1 (mannose receptor C-type 1, a M2 macrophage marker) in the colon. Mice of the DSS + F5 group exhibited decreased mRNA expression of MRC1compared with mice of DSS+PBS or DSS+F5+polyamines ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 E ). A similar alteration in the CD206: F4/80 ratio in the colon was observed among groups, indicating a lower ratio of M2 macrophages in DSS+F5 group ( Fig. 6 H ). Collectively, the lower population of M2 macrophages induced by F5 may contribute to the delay in colitis recovery.

Although lower level of polyamines delays the recovery of colitis, increased levels of polyamines caused by enhanced biosynthesis are associated with the pathogenesis of cancers in skin, breast, colon, lung, prostate, and pancreas ( 21 ). Activation of mTOR in prostate cancer results in high levels of AMD1 and polyamines ( 2 ). Notably, inhibiting polyamine biosynthesis by ODC1 inhibition prevents CRC growth ( 22 ). Although we have revealed the role of gut microbiota-derived small RNAs in host polyamine metabolism, the potential translational significance of this result in CRC remains unclear. The majority of researchers choose chemical induction models to study the occurrence and development of CRC in animal models, especially AOM-DSS ( 23 – 25 ), we therefore used our previous established mouse model of CRC with AOM/DSS treatment ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 F ) ( 26 ). There was a considerable reduction in the expression of sR-182871, sR-242825, and sR-257800 in the colon of mice with CRC ( Fig. 6 I ). Meanwhile, elevated mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM ( Fig. 6 J ), and polyamine levels ( Fig. 6 K ) were observed in the colon of mice with CRC. These results suggest that the intestinal microbiota-derived small RNAs-polyamine metabolism axis is involved in the pathogenesis of CRC.

To translate our findings to clinical implications, we analyzed the published CRC metabolomic data in the serum ( 27 ) and feces ( 28 ). Interestingly, compared to the healthy controls, there was a substantially increased level of spermidine in serum of patients with CRC ( Fig. 6 L and M ). Elevated level of spermine in the feces of patients with CRC, especially in stage I/II CRC classification, was also observed compared with that of healthy individuals ( Fig. 6 N and O ). Interestingly, we found considerably lower level of total polyamines in normal individuals with a history of colorectal surgery compared with patients with CRC ( Fig. 6 N and O ). These results indicate that polyamine metabolism is dysregulated in CRC.

Next, we collected the CRC specimens (CRCs) and paracancerous normal-appearing colorectal tissue specimens (PNACTs) from patients with CRC ( Fig. 6 P ). We compared the abundance of Lactobacillus and L. murinus in CRCs and PNACTs and found an increased abundance of Lactobacillus in CRCs ( Fig. 6 Q ), which is consistent with the previous study ( 29 ). Meanwhile, based on the previous method to detect L. murinus in the human feces ( 30 ), a lower abundance of L. murinus was detected in CRCs ( Fig. 6 R ). Consistently, a decline in abundance of sR-182871, sR-242825, and sR-257800 was observed in CRCs ( Fig. 6 S ), which was accompanied by elevated expression of enzymes in polyamine metabolism ( Fig. 6 T and U ) and increased polyamine levels ( Fig. 6 V ). Collectively, these results suggest that the intestinal microbiota-derived small RNAs-host polyamine metabolism axis is associated with the pathogenesis of CRC.
sections.discussion:
Compelling results indicate that polyamines incorporate into vital physiological processes, including life-span extension, tumorigenesis, neuroprotection, and inflammation ( 5 , 31 – 33 ). However, little is known about the precise molecular mechanisms of the modulation of polyamine metabolism, especially concerning the gut microbiota. Here, we revealed that gut microbiota regulates polyamine metabolism of the host ( Fig. 7 ). However, we found that the levels of putrescine and spermine in the serum of germ-free mice were significantly higher than those of SPF mice ( Fig. 1 B ), but no corresponding changes were observed in germ-free pigs ( Fig. 1 A ). This may be due to the inherent species differences in genetics and physiology, which will cause metabolic and physiological differences between pig and mice ( 34 ). For example, the blood glucose level of pigs is significantly lower than that of mice, and there are also differences in bile acid profiles ( 35 ). However, further experiments are needed to investigate the differences in polyamine metabolism between pigs and mice at other organ and tissue levels.

The graphic summary of this study. Germ-free pigs have elevated polyamine levels in the colon because intestinal L. murinus -derived small RNAs in extracellular vesicles down-regulate host polyamine metabolism by inhibiting the expression of enzymes in polyamine metabolism.

Previous studies have demonstrated that specific gut microbes are critical to modulate host metabolism. For instance, Bacteroides vulgatus decreases mouse tauroursodeoxycholic acid ( 36 ); Bifidobacterium longum CCFM1029 up-regulates host tryptophan metabolism ( 37 ). In this study, we identified that L. murinus down-regulates the polyamine levels in the colon of mice. Interestingly, we also found a significant positive correlation between Streptococcus lutetiensis and polyamines; however, it is unclear whether the increased polyamine level in the colistin-treated group is related to S. lutetiensis .

Gut microbes influence host physiology mainly through metabolites or bacterial components. For instance, indoles ( 38 ), trimethylamine N-oxide ( 39 ), 4-ethylphenol (4-EP) ( 40 ), and bile acids ( 41 ) from bacteria are reported to modulate host physiology. Notably, pasteurization of Akkmernsia. muciniphila ( A. muciniphila ) is reported to enhance its capacity to reduce fat mass development, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia in mice ( 42 ). In particular, Amuc_1100 isolated from the outer membrane of A. muciniphila partly recapitulates the beneficial effects of the bacterium ( 42 ). Here, we found that F5-derived small RNAs decrease the mRNA expression of ODC1, AMD1, and SRM, as well as polyamine levels. Small RNAs are a class of regulatory noncoding RNAs, which regulate vital biological processes by regulating gene expression in a particular fashion ( 43 ). MicroRNAs show stable expression in the serum and plasma of humans and other animals ( 44 ) and the property of boiling water resistance ( 45 ). Notably, accumulating evidence indicate that small RNAs can transmit across species. For instance, microRNAs from the parasitic plant Cuscuta campestris act as trans-species regulator of host-gene expression ( 46 ). In addition, Wong-Bajracharya et al. provide evidence of small RNA transferring from ectomycorrhizal fungi to plant roots, shedding light on the involvement of miRNAs during the developmental process of mutualistic symbioses ( 47 ). However, no examples of naturally occurring trans-species small RNAs targeting host polyamine metabolism have been described for bacteria–host interactions.

CRC is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, and its incidence is increasing ( 48 , 49 ). The formation of CRC is multifactorial, including genetic factors typically exemplified by familial adenomatous polyposis, while they account for a minority of CRC cases. Indeed, up to 90% of disease risk is thought to be due to environmental factors ( 50 ). Among environmental factors, the role of microorganisms in cancer biology has been increasingly recognized ( 51 ). The pathogenesis of CRC related to gut microbiota typically involves inflammation, immune regulation, metabolism of dietary components, and genotoxin production ( 52 ). For instance, colibactin-producing polyketide synthase (pks) + Escherichia coli induce double-strand breaks, aneuploidy, and improper cellular division ( 53 ). In addition, a higher relative abundance of Fusobacterium nucleatum and Bacteroides fragili detected in the CRC tumor tissue ( 50 , 54 , 55 ) contribute to the development of CRC through inflammation, intestinal barrier failure, and accumulation of somatic oncogenic mutations ( 56 – 58 ). In our study, we found elevated polyamine levels in the colon of mice with CRC and patients with CRC, accompanied by a lower abundance of L. murinus and L. murinus -derived small RNAs. Interestingly, we showed that the lower abundance of L. murinus in CRCs was accompanied by an up-regulation of the total Lactobacillus abundance, which may be related to the antagonistic interactions among strains in a complex environment ( 59 , 60 ).
